data.heading: Form of the Passive
bullets: We often use the passive (be + past participle) when it isn't said, known, or important who does an action.

Examples: 'A lot of films are shot on location.' 'The director died when the film was being made.' 'When is our car being repaired?' 'You'll be picked up at the airport by one of our staff.' 'This bill must be paid tomorrow.' 'I love being given a massage.' 'The new concert hall will be opened by the King.'
In passive sentences, the object of the verb becomes the new subject: 'Artem's bike has been stolen.' (Somebody has stolen Artem's bike, but we don't know who.)

narr: The passive voice is formed using the verb 'be' plus the past participle of the main verb. We use this construction when the person performing the action is unknown, unimportant, or when we want to emphasize the object of the action rather than the doer.

For example, in 'A lot of films are shot on location,' the focus is on the films, not on who shot them. Similarly, 'When is our car being repaired?' emphasizes the car being repaired, not who is doing the repairing.

A key characteristic of passive sentences is that the object of the active sentence becomes the new subject. In 'Artem's bike has been stolen,' the bike is now the subject of the sentence, while the person who stole it is not mentioned.

data.heading: Use of the Passive
bullets: (a) To move important information—the object of the active sentence—to the beginning of the sentence: 'Two men are being questioned by the police.'
(b) To be impersonal and not mention the name of the person who performs the action
(c) When it is obvious who performed the action (e.g. teachers), or when we do not want to use a general subject such as 'people' or 'someone'

narr: The passive voice has several important uses in English. First, we use it to move important information to the beginning of the sentence. For example, 'Two men are being questioned by the police' puts the focus on the men rather than the police.

Second, the passive allows us to be impersonal by not mentioning who performs the action. This is particularly useful in scientific or technical writing, such as 'Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea,' where the focus is on the resources rather than the finders.
Third, we use the passive when it's obvious who performed the action, like when teachers assign homework, or when we want to avoid using vague subjects like 'people' or 'someone'.

data.heading: The Agent By
bullets: Use 'by' when it's important to know who performed the action
Only use 'by' when it's really necessary to identify the agent
Examples: Some countries have been harmed by tourism. Many buildings have been damaged by the earthquake.

narr: First, let's talk about the agent 'by'.
We use 'by' when we want to specify who performed the action in a passive sentence.
For instance, we might say 'Some countries have been harmed by tourism' to identify tourism as the harming agent.
However, we only use 'by' when it's really necessary to identify the agent.
In cases where the agent is obvious, we can omit it. For example, 'The two men were arrested' - it's obvious that the police made the arrest.

data.heading: Active or Passive - Two Ways of Focusing
bullets: We can express the same idea in active or passive voice
The choice depends on what we want to focus on
Example: Napoleon was directed by Ridley Scott (focus on the film) / Ridley Scott directed Napoleon (focus on the director)

narr: English offers us two ways to express the same idea: active and passive voice.
The choice between them depends on what we want to emphasize.
For example, if we want to focus more on the film, we might say 'Napoleon was directed by Ridley Scott'.
But if we want to focus more on the director, we'd say 'Ridley Scott directed Napoleon'.

data.heading: Forming Negatives and Questions in Passive Voice
bullets: Negatives and questions are formed similarly to active sentences
Add 'not' after the appropriate form of 'be'
For questions, invert the subject and the appropriate form of 'be'

narr: When forming negatives and questions in passive voice, the process is similar to active sentences.
For negatives, we simply add 'not' after the appropriate form of 'be'.
For example, 'Some films aren't shot on location.'
For questions, we invert the subject and the appropriate form of 'be', like 'Is your car being repaired today?'

data.heading: Present Simple Passive
bullets: Form: am/is/are + past participle
Used for processes that are generally true
Examples: Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea. This room isn't used very often.

narr: Let's look at the present simple passive voice.
Its form is 'am/is/are' plus the past participle of the main verb.
We use it for processes that are generally true or habitual.
For example, 'Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea' describes a general truth.
Similarly, 'This room isn't used very often' describes a habitual situation.

data.heading: Past Simple Passive
bullets: Form: was/were + past participle
Used for finished events in the past
Examples: The college was built in the 16th century. Aztec boys were trained to fight.

narr: Now for the past simple passive voice.
Its form is 'was/were' plus the past participle of the main verb.
We use it to describe finished events in the past.
For instance, 'The college was built in the 16th century' refers to a completed action.
Another example is 'Aztec boys were trained to fight', describing a past practice.

data.heading: Transitive and Intransitive Verbs
bullets: Transitive verbs have an object
Intransitive verbs don't have an object
Only transitive verbs can be made passive

narr: To understand passive voice better, we need to know about transitive and intransitive verbs.
Transitive verbs have an object - like in 'I lost my wallet on the way to school', where 'wallet' is the object.
Intransitive verbs don't have an object, like in 'I swim every day'.
Here's an important rule: only transitive verbs can be made passive.

data.heading: The Preposition With
bullets: Use 'with' for objects which perform actions
Example: The game was played with a ball of solid rubber

narr: Another useful structure is the preposition 'with'.
We use 'with' for objects that perform actions in passive sentences.
For example, 'The game was played with a ball of solid rubber' - here the ball is performing the action of playing.

data.heading: The Passive in Science and Engineering
bullets: Often used to talk about processes
The steps of the process matter more than the person doing them
Examples from manufacturing: A hole is made using a drill. A material is pressed into the correct shape.
Examples from science: Around 25% is reflected by the upper atmosphere. Finally, 50% is absorbed by the Earth's surface.

narr: In science and engineering, we frequently use the passive voice.
This is because we want to focus on the process itself rather than who performs it.
For example, in manufacturing descriptions, we might say 'A hole is made using a drill' or 'A material is pressed into the correct shape'.
Similarly, in scientific contexts, we might say 'Around 25% is reflected by the upper atmosphere' or '50% is absorbed by the Earth's surface'.

data.heading: Sequencing a Process
bullets: Use adverbs to show sequence: firstly, then, next, after that, finally
Use words to show relationships: after, as, as soon as, once, when
Use 'at this stage' to create a clear sequence

narr: When describing processes, we need ways to sequence events.
First, we can use adverbs like 'firstly', 'then', 'next', 'after that', and 'finally'.
For example, 'Firstly, some energy is removed by the clouds.'
We can also use words like 'after', 'as', 'as soon as', 'once', and 'when' to show how events relate to each other.
Like in 'As soon as sunlight hits the flower, its petals open.'
Additionally, we use phrases like 'at this stage' to create a clear sequence, such as 'The temperature reaches 100°C. At this stage, the water begins to boil.'

rows.text: We find oil and gas beneath the ground or sea.
Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea.
The police are questioning two men.
Two men are being questioned by the police.
Teachers trained Aztec boys to fight.
Aztec boys were trained to fight.

narr: Let's compare active and passive forms across different tenses.
In the present simple, we have 'We find oil and gas' in active voice versus 'Oil and gas are found' in passive.
For present continuous, it's 'The police are questioning two men' versus 'Two men are being questioned by the police'.
In past simple, we see 'Teachers trained Aztec boys' versus 'Aztec boys were trained'.
For present perfect, we have 'Tourism has harmed some countries' versus 'Some countries have been harmed by tourism'.
And with future tense using 'will', it's 'We will choose a new class representative' versus 'A new class representative will be chosen'.

data.heading: Active vs. Passive Voice

data.heading: Types of Charts and Diagrams
bullets: Pie chart: A circle divided into segments from the middle (like slices of a cake), with a key or legend showing what each segment represents
Bar chart: Thin vertical or horizontal bars of the same width whose height or length varies with the amounts
Cross-section: Something cut across the middle so that you can see the inside
Flowchart: A diagram which indicates the stages of a process
Table: A grid with columns and rows of numbers

narr: There are various types of charts and diagrams used in engineering to represent data.
First, let's consider the pie chart.
A pie chart is essentially a circle divided into segments from the middle, resembling slices of a cake.
Each segment represents a portion of the whole, and a key or legend explains what each segment represents.
Next, we have the bar chart.
A bar chart consists of thin vertical or horizontal bars of the same width.
The height or length of these bars varies according to the amounts they represent.
For showing different layers of rock, like in the Grand Canyon, a cross-section is most appropriate.
A cross-section shows something cut across the middle, allowing you to see the inside structure.
When presenting different stages in a process, such as a research project, a flowchart is ideal.
A flowchart diagram indicates the various stages of a process and how they connect.
Finally, tables are fundamental for organizing numerical data.
A table is essentially a grid with columns and rows of numbers.
Columns run vertically from top to bottom, while rows run horizontally across the table.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Family Car Depreciation
data.problem: The average family car in the UK goes down in value by 20% per year. This means its value has fallen by more than half after just three years.
data.result: After three years, the car retains 51.2% of its original value, meaning it has depreciated by 48.8%, which is indeed more than half.

narr: Let's examine how car depreciation works mathematically.
If a car loses 20% of its value each year, it retains 80% of its value annually.
After one year, the car is worth 80% of its original value.
After two years, it's worth 80% of the previous year's value, which is 64% of the original.
After three years, it's worth 80% of the second year's value, which is 51.2% of the original.
This means the car has lost 48.8% of its value after three years, confirming that it has depreciated by more than half.

data.heading: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
bullets: Physiological needs

narr: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a theory of psychological health predicated on fulfilling innate human needs in priority order.
The hierarchy is often visualized as a pyramid with the most basic needs at the bottom.
Physiological needs like food, water, and shelter must be satisfied first.
Once these are met, safety needs such as job security and a stable salary become important.
Next come belonging needs, then esteem needs, and finally self-actualization at the top.

narr: Let's answer our first question about Maslow's hierarchy.
Which need is fulfilled first?
The answer lies in understanding the structure of the pyramid.
The needs are arranged in order of priority, with the most basic needs at the bottom.
Physiological needs, such as food, water, and shelter, must be satisfied before any other needs can motivate behavior.
Therefore, the needs at the bottom of the pyramid — the basic, physiological needs — are fulfilled first.

narr: Our next question asks if we can skip directly from security needs to esteem needs.
The answer is no, and here's why.
Maslow's hierarchy operates in a specific sequence.
Security needs are the second level from the bottom.
Esteem needs are the fourth level, just below self-actualization.
Between security and esteem are belonging needs, which must be satisfied before esteem needs can become motivators.
Therefore, we cannot move directly from security needs to esteem needs.

narr: Now let's explore what happens when one need is met.
According to Maslow's theory, once a need is satisfied, it ceases to be a primary motivator.
The focus then shifts to the next higher level need in the hierarchy.
This creates a progression up the pyramid as each need is fulfilled.
Therefore, when one need is met, the next level up becomes the main motivator, and the person moves up the pyramid.

data.heading: Task 5, question 2.4

narr: Our final question addresses whether everyone must reach the top of the pyramid to be satisfied.
The answer is no, and this is an important aspect of Maslow's theory.
Self-actualization, the top level, represents the full realization of a person's potential.
However, this may not be achievable or necessary for everyone to experience satisfaction in life.
People can find fulfillment and satisfaction at various levels of the hierarchy depending on their circumstances, values, and life experiences.
Therefore, not everyone reaches self-actualization, and people can be satisfied at different levels.

data.heading: Word Formation Techniques
bullets: Suffixes: added to the end of verbs or adjectives to form nouns
Prefixes: added to the beginning of words to change meaning
Roots: core meaning of word family with affixes added around it
Compound nouns: combination of two nouns written as one expression
Conversion: word changes its job without changing its shape

narr: Word formation techniques are methods used to create new words from existing ones.
Suffixes are added to the end of verbs or adjectives to form nouns, like turning 'act' into 'action' using the suffix '-tion'.
Prefixes are added to the beginning of words and typically change meaning, often making a word negative or indicating reversal.
Roots form the core meaning of a word family, with affixes added around them, like 'inspect' becoming 'inspector' and then 'inspection'.
Compound nouns combine two nouns into one expression, written as a single unit.
Conversion is unique because a word changes its grammatical function without any change in form, like 'email' being both a noun and a verb.

data.heading: Suffix Examples
bullets: -tion: act → action, inspect → inspection
-ment: develop → development, measure → measurement
-ness: happy → happiness, dark → darkness
-ity: able → ability, possible → possibility
-er: build → builder, design → designer
-or: act → actor, generate → generator

narr: Let's examine noun-forming suffixes in more detail.
The suffix '-tion' turns verbs into nouns, like 'act' becoming 'action' or 'inspect' becoming 'inspection'.
The suffix '-ment' also converts verbs to nouns, as in 'develop' to 'development' or 'measure' to 'measurement'.
The suffix '-ness' typically turns adjectives into nouns, such as 'happy' to 'happiness' or 'dark' to 'darkness'.
The suffix '-ity' converts adjectives to nouns, like 'able' to 'ability' or 'possible' to 'possibility'.

The suffixes '-er' and '-or' both turn verbs into nouns that represent people, with '-er' used for many verbs like 'build' to 'builder' or 'design' to 'designer', while '-or' is used for others like 'act' to 'actor' or 'generate' to 'generator'.

data.heading: Conversion - Zero Derivation
bullets: Word changes its job without changing its shape
No prefix or suffix is added
Common pattern: noun to verb
Also common: verb to noun

narr: Conversion is a fascinating word formation technique where a word changes its grammatical function without any change in form.
Unlike other methods, we add no prefix or suffix - the word simply starts working as a different part of speech.
This is why teachers sometimes call it 'zero derivation', because the ending is essentially zero.
The most common conversion pattern is from noun to verb, as in 'email' - 'I got an email' versus 'Email me tomorrow'.
Verb to noun conversion is also very frequent, as in 'run' - 'I run every day' versus 'I went for a run'.

data.heading: Conversion Examples

narr: Let's look at some common examples of conversion in English.
First, the noun 'email' can become a verb: 'I got an email' versus 'Email me tomorrow'.
Similarly, 'phone' functions as both a noun and verb: 'My phone is new' versus 'I'll phone you tonight'.
The word 'book' works as both a noun and verb: 'I'm reading a book' versus 'We booked a table'.

Conversion also works in reverse from verb to noun: 'I run every day' versus 'I went for a run'.
These examples demonstrate how conversion allows English to be efficient with vocabulary, as one word can serve multiple functions.

bullets: 1. Where is it? After articles/adjectives = noun; after subject/to/will/can/must = verb

narr: To determine which class a word belongs to, ask three questions. First, where is it in the sentence? After articles or adjectives, it's likely a noun; after a subject or modals like 'to', 'will', 'can', it's probably a verb. Second, can it change form? Verbs can take suffixes like '-s', '-ed', '-ing', while nouns take articles or plural '-s'. Third, does the stress move? Some two-syllable words change stress between noun and verb forms.
Some words change stress between noun and verb forms. For example, 'a REcord' versus 'to reCORD'. The noun stress is on the first syllable, while the verb stress shifts to the second syllable.

narr: Here's a quick reference table for passive voice forms.
In the present simple passive, we use 'am/is/are' plus the past participle, as in 'Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea.'
For present continuous passive, we use 'am/is/are being' plus the past participle: 'Two men are being questioned by the police.'
Past simple passive uses 'was/were' plus past participle: 'Aztec boys were trained to fight.'
Present perfect passive employs 'has/have been' plus past participle: 'Some countries have been harmed by tourism.'
Future passive uses 'will be' plus past participle: 'A new class representative will be chosen on Monday.'
When we need to specify who performed the action, we use 'by' plus the agent, but only when it's really necessary.
For instruments that perform the action, we use 'with' plus the object: 'The game was played with a ball of solid rubber.'
Remember that only transitive verbs can be made passive, and negatives and questions are formed just like in active sentences.

narr: Here's a comprehensive table of verb and noun plus preposition patterns.
For verbs like 'increase' and 'decrease', we use 'by' to indicate the size of change: 'The population of the city has increased by 10%.'
When these words are nouns, we use 'of' for the size or 'in' for what's changing: 'a rise of 15% in the number of cars.'
For 'effect' and 'impact', we use 'on': 'The effect of the film on the audience was very powerful.'
With 'reason', we use 'for' or 'why': 'What was the reason for his success?'
For 'precedent', we use 'for': 'There are several precedents for taking such a decision.'
The verb 'contribute' takes 'to': 'Mobile technology contributed to the information revolution.'
Words like 'stem' and 'spring' use 'from': 'Sid's determination stems from his desire to improve.'
The verb 'account' uses 'for': 'The tilting of the earth accounts for the change in seasons.'
The phrase 'give rise' takes 'to': 'The victory gave rise to a new mood.'
The verb 'derive' uses 'from': 'Benefits can be derived from this situation.'
Interestingly, 'influence' as a verb takes no preposition: 'Her grandmother influenced Sarah's choice.'
Finally, phrases like 'reach a peak' or 'exceed' have specific patterns: 'The amount reaches a peak at 18.'

narr: Here's a table showing common suffixes used for noun formation.
The suffix '-tion' is added to verbs to create nouns: 'act' becomes 'action', 'inspect' becomes 'inspection'.
Similarly, '-ment' turns verbs into nouns: 'develop' becomes 'development', 'measure' becomes 'measurement'.
For adjectives, we use '-ness' to form nouns: 'happy' becomes 'happiness', 'dark' becomes 'darkness'.
The suffix '-ity' also works with adjectives: 'able' becomes 'ability', 'possible' becomes 'possibility'.
When added to verbs, '-er' creates agent nouns: 'build' becomes 'builder', 'design' becomes 'designer'.
The suffix '-or' serves a similar function: 'act' becomes 'actor', 'generate' becomes 'generator'.
From the course, we've also seen examples like 'motivate → motivation', 'influence → influence', 'trigger → trigger', 'contribute → contribution', and 'induce → inducement'.
Finally, remember that conversion adds nothing at all to the word—it's simply using a different part of speech, like 'water' (noun) becoming 'to water' (verb).

For example, 'Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea' focuses on what is found, not who found it.
Similarly, 'a hole is made using a drill' emphasizes the action and the tool, not the person operating the drill.
